It sucked at his arms, pulled his body down, soaked cloth clinging against his skin. He gasped and fumbled with the zipper, yanking the jacket loose and letting it drift free in the water. It wasn’t that much of a loss — the Fog would return it at the campfire like everything else the survivors left behind — but he still felt exposed without it. The ceiling was maybe 2 feet above the water now, maybe less, the space between the surface and the plaster shrinking steadily. He kept his eyes on it anyway — not that looking helped, the flashlight beam barely reaching the pipes directly ahead of them — and tried not to think about what it meant that he could feel the cold air on the top of his head. The flashlight buzzed. The bulb flickered, dimmed, flared again like it was coughing. It had never been good, but the periodic submersions had taken something fundamental out of it — the beam guttering now when it should have held steady, throwing the ceiling into shadow for a half second at a time before catching again. Dwight held it above the surface as much as he could manage, which wasn't always, and every time it went under, he felt the weight of the dark press in a little closer. He was starting to lose track of where the hole should be. The hallway had shifted so much from its original shape that nothing lined up anymore — no landmark he'd clocked on the first pass was where he expected it to be, and the ceiling above them was uniform and featureless in the failing beam. What if She'd closed it? What if the geometry had swallowed it entirely, the way it had swallowed the extra distance and the extra junctions and the logic of the space itself? Dwight shook off the thought, blinked hard and adjusted the angle. He had been sweeping the ceiling in slow arcs, watching the plaster slide past in the weak yellow light, when the texture changed — torn edges framing a gap that swallowed the beam entirely, a circle of absolute black that stretched the full width of the hallway above them. “There!” he shouted, voice cracking with hope and desperation. “There it is!” David looked up with a half-relieved laugh just as the flashlight gave its last pathetic breath. A final, stuttering flick of yellow that haloed the hole for barely a second... And died. The dark swallowed them. No noise. No light. Just breath and water and the dizzying pressure of a space that no longer wanted them. “Shit – no no no...” Dwight shook the flashlight, trying to will it back to life. The current dragged at his hips and his elbow hit a pipe, the flashlight popping free of his grasp and lazily drifting towards the floor. “Dwight?” “I’ve got it! I—” He flailed, slipped under for a second, and broke the surface again coughing. David's hand found his collar and hauled him back up, hard enough to hurt. “You don’t got it,” David snapped. “I’m fine,” Dwight choked out, blinking water from his eyes. He could still see the hole in his mind — could still remember the angle — but now there was only black. "David, the light - I can't..." “Just leave it! Come on. The hole was right there. Feel around! It spanned the whole hallway. It’s not like we can miss it.” Dwight tipped his head back. The ceiling was right there — he could feel the cold air against his face, barely a foot of space between the water's surface and the plaster. He reached up and his fingers found it immediately. Dwight hesitated in the dark for a moment before slamming his palm against the ceiling, clinging to the pipes on the wall for stability as the two scrambled down the hall towards where they had last seen the edge. They moved by touch, hands flat against the ceiling, the current tugging at their legs with that same gentle insistence that had followed them through the whole hallway. Dwight counted his strokes. Fifteen feet, maybe less. They'd seen it. It was right there. The ceiling slid under his palms, unbroken and smooth, telling him nothing. — They went under together. One moment there was still an inch of air, the cold plaster brushing the tops of their heads, and then there wasn't — the surface closing the last gap with a quiet finality. No rush. No drama. Just the ceiling arriving, and the space gone, and the dark complete in every direction at once. The current had been waiting for exactly this — the moment neither of them had a surface to orient by — and it pulled with more confidence now, a slow lateral drag that had no interest in where they wanted to go. He kept one hand on the ceiling, pulling himself forward through the dark, counting his strokes the way he'd been counting since the flashlight died. The hole had been fifteen feet ahead, maybe less. He'd seen it. He knew where it was. At some point he realized he couldn't feel David anymore. Not a dramatic separation — no collision, no moment of loss. Just the gradual awareness that the presence he'd been tracking by sound and movement and the occasional brush of an arm had gone quiet, and the vibrations in the water were coming from somewhere he couldn't locate, muffled and directionless in the dark. He swept a hand out to the side and found nothing but water. Dwight didn’t mean to lose track of him. But the bizarre current, however slow it seemed, tugged him just wrong. Or maybe it was panic. Maybe it was the weight of soaked clothes and adrenaline
